idiom_name: value-returning method contract (result, previous value, outcome, or receiver) with an explicit discard
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: before writing the body, decide what the caller is expected to do with the outcome and return exactly that - the created or updated object, the value that was replaced, a boolean or enum saying what changed, a status/result carrying failure, or the receiver for a fluent step. Where the language defaults to returning nothing, the return type is the only place the contract can live, so write it explicitly and mark results that must not be dropped with whatever the toolchain offers (attribute, lint or type). Conversely, when there is genuinely nothing interesting to report, return nothing at all: a fabricated value teaches callers that return values are noise. Beck's rule is the whole pattern: return a value when you intend the sender to use it - and make that intention visible both in the signature and at the call site.
code_sketch:
result = map.put(key, value)          # the value that was replaced
added  = set.add(item)                # did anything change?
builder.append(x).append(y).build()   # receiver returned for chaining
value, err = parse(text)              # the outcome carries failure
obj.tap { log(obj) }                  # receiver returned for a side step
pitfalls: Returning a value from a method whose result is meaningless, so callers learn to ignore return values generally.
Two methods that both mutate state but only one returns a value, leaving callers unable to tell why.
Letting whatever expression happens to be last become the method's public return value by accident.
Returning a meaningless placeholder (true, self, OK) from a side-effect-only method: callers cannot distinguish noise from signal and eventually ignore all return values from that API surface.

Chaining receiver-returning mutators across more than three levels obscures the intermediate values being passed through, making stack-traces and debugger stepping harder to follow than a plain sequential statement would be.

Overloading a fluent setter with a query that also returns the set value (C++ operator= returns *this, Java getters return void by convention): a reader cannot tell from the call site whether a given line is a query or a command without reading the method declaration.

Marking a result nodiscard/must_use but also designing it to be legitimately ignored in the majority of call sites, which trains developers to suppress or cast away the warning universally and defeats the safety purpose.

Returning a raw internal pointer or mutable reference as the 'interesting' value, breaking encapsulation by exposing the object's internal buffer or cursor to callers who then depend on representation details.

Wrong move: return self from every mutator solely to make call sites chainable -> the result carries no new information, blurs command/query intent, and makes accidental train-wreck chains look valid -> instead return the actual outcome or keep the method void.

Wrong move: discard a partial-result/error pair because an error is present -> APIs such as Go's io.Reader can return n > 0 together with err, so dropping the return value loses work and failure context -> instead consume the value before handling the error.

Wrong move: return only a boolean when the caller needs the produced value -> the caller must re-query or use a side channel, restoring the race and duplication the pattern avoids -> instead return the value with explicit absence or error (for example, an Option/Result or typed pair).
